    12   ABSTRACT
    13    This study explored the efficiency of CO2-, N2-, and H2- nanobubble treatment in anaerobic
    14    digestion (AD) of rice straw, with a focus on the processes and metabolic pathways of
    15    hydrolytic acidification, and revealed the underlying mechanisms. Mechanistic investigations
    16   revealed  that nanobubbles,  particularly CO2 nanobubbles,  significantly  increased  the
    17   degradation of amorphous cellulose, resulting in higher levels of soluble carbohydrates (6.27%
    18   – 11.13%), VFAs (4.39% – 24.50%), and a remarkable cumulative H2 yield (74 – 94 times)
    19    Microbial community analysis indicated that the CO2 nanobubble promoted the growth of
    20    acidifying bacterial communities, such as Mobilitalea, unclassified_f_Lachnospiraceae, and
    21    Bacteroides. This indicates that the introduction of CO2 nanobubbles improved the total
    22   abundance of predicted functional enzymes were increased by 14%, resulting  in the
    23   production of more easily degradable intermediates. Based on the analysis of total methane
    24   production and kinetic analysis, it can be concluded that nanobubble addition enhanced
    25   methane production levels of 4.22% - 7.79% with lower lag time (λ) (0.88–1.06 day) compared
    26   to the control group (1.09 day). The results also elucidated changes in relative enzymatic
    27    activities involved in the bioconversion of cellulose and hemicellulose during the hydrolysis
    28   stage with nanobubble treatment. This work  is more beneficial for understanding the
    29   promoting effect and mechanism of nanobubbles on AD, facilitating the more precise
    30    application of nanobubble technology in the field of renewable energy.
    31   Keywords: bioresources recovery, hydrolytic acidification, micro-nanobubble technology,
    32   renewable energy, rice straw, sustainable waste management

    33   1. Introduction
    34   The escalating global demand  for sustainable and renewable resources has attracted
    35    significant interest in utilising biomass waste as a valuable raw material for bioresource

36   recovery [1]. Rice cultivation sustains a significant portion of the global population and
37   generates approximately 1062 million tons of agricultural residues annually in the form of rice
38    straw, which is a typical lignocellulosic biomass [2,3]. Conventional disposal methods for the
39    lignocellulosic biomass, such as open field burning or landfills, contribute to air pollution and
40    result in the loss of valuable organic matter and nutrients [4]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) of rice
41   straw has been developed and widely recognized as a promising approach for producing biogas
42   and nutrient-rich fertilizer [5]. Moreover, AD can promote climate change mitigation, sustain a
43    circular economy on farms, and contribute to the attainment of the global net zero target[6].
44    Rice straw, a lignocellulosic biomass, exhibits a complex fibre structure resulting from the
45    intricate cross-linking of lignocellulose into highly polymerized crystals [7]. Lignocellulosic
46   biomass exhibits lower biodegradability compared with other organics such as carbohydrates.
47    Therefore, the CH4 yield from the AD of lignocellulosic biomass accounts for less 60% of its
48    theoretical potential [8]. As known, the hydrolysis process, which is the initial step in the AD
49    process, imposes constraints on the conversion of lignocellulosic materials into desirable end
50   products [8]. Researchers have made several efforts to enhance the AD performance of rice
51    straw, including pre-treating the materials to disrupt the lignocellulosic structure [9], microbial
52   augmentation by adding specific bacterial cultures during the AD process [10], and co-
53    digestion of rice straw with manure feedstocks [11]. However, the shortcomings of these
54   approaches become evident when they are applied. For example, potentially hazardous
55   byproducts, including 5-hydroxymethylfurfural, furfural, and phenolic compounds, may arise
56    following acid pretreatment, particularly under elevated temperatures [12]. In order to avoid
57   secondary pollution, certain adsorption methods or adsorbents are also needed [13].
58   Improper handling of adsorbents can also cause pollution and increase treatment costs. Hence,
59   developing a novel intensification approach that requires fewer chemical additives and proves
60   to be more cost-effective and efficient is vital.
61   Nanobubbles refer to bubbles with a diameter of less than 1 µm, and their existence was
62   experimentally confirmed via atomic force microscopy imaging in 2000 [14]. In addition to
63    their small size and large surface area, nanobubbles exhibit other unique characteristics such
64   as remarkable longevity, low buoyancy, a negative surface charge, and the ability to generate
65    reactive oxygen species (ROSs, e.g., •OH, H2O2, and O2-) [15]. As an emerging technology,
66   nanobubbles have been used to address environmental issues since 2004, with the first
67   attempt to enhance AD performance using nanobubbles occurring in 2019. Wang and Yang
68    [16] added a solution of air, N2, CO2, and H2-filled nanobubbles to the AD of waste activated
69   sludge and achieved a 14% – 21% improvement in CH4 production.
70   For AD of lignocellulosic biomass (Table 1), several studies have been demonstrated that using
71   nanobubble solutions as the additives can significantly increase CH4 production by up to 29%
72    in AD of variable lignocellulosic feedstocks (Table 1). The direct pre-treatment of the feedstock

73    rice straw with different nanobubbles (N2, O2 and CO2) led to a significant enhancement in
74    volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production from 1873.3 (control) to 5889.6 mg·L-1 (CO2-nanobubble)
75    [17]. A previous study demonstrated that the addition of nanobubble solution during the AD
76    of food waste could enhance the enzymatic activity and increase the VFAs yields by 6-18% in
77    hydrolytic acidification process [18]. Wang and Yuan [19] reported that the introduction of N2-
78   nanobubbles enhanced cellulase activities by 12.6% during the AD of corn straw, thereby
79   improving the degradation of crystalline cellulose by microorganisms. Song and Hou [20] found
80    that the addition of CO2-nanobubble enhanced β-glucosidase and dehydrogenase activities
81   and improved corn straw hydrolysis, which could further promote a 17% increase in the
82   maximum methane yield. Furthermore, CO2 and air nanobubbles enriched the microbial
83   community of hydrolysis and acidification bacteria, such as Aminicenantes and Spirochaetae
84    [21]. Wang and Yuan [19] showed that the nanobubble treatment groups exhibited a higher
85    relative abundance of Thermotoga, Chloroflexi, Bacteroidetes, Spirochaetae, Synergistetes,
86   and Firmicutes than the control group. However, there have been no reports on systematic
87   microscopic studies of the mechanism of nanobubbles as additives in the AD process of
88    lignocellulosic materials.

91   To address the knowledge gaps, this study investigated the effects and mechanisms of
92   nanobubble technology in enhancing the hydrolysis-acidification stage of AD of rice straw. First,
93   the mechanisms and consequences of N2, H2, and CO2 nanobubble treatments on specific
94    hydrolysis-acidification process were evaluated, and the final products in the solid, liquid, and
95   gas forms the hydrolysis and acidification phases were quantified. Additionally, the relative

96   abundance of bacteria and the activity of key enzymes during the hydrolysis-acidification of
 97    rice straw by treatment of CO2-nanobubble were analysed to elucidate the mechanism of CO2-
 98   nanobubble on hydrolysis and acidogenesis process. Furthermore, different kinetic models
 99   were used to describe the basic mechanisms. This study aims to elucidate the mechanism of
100   nanobubble technology to facilitate the AD approach for sustainable bioresource recovery and
101   renewable energy generation.

102   2. Materials and methods
103    2.1. Materials
104    Rice straw was gathered from the Lianshui County, Jiangsu Province, China, and then dried at
105   105 °C before crushed for 2 minutes. The main characteristics of the rice straw were as follows:
106    cellulose (36.03 ± 0.6%), hemicellulose (29.60 ± 0.15%), and lignin (4.78 ± 0.38%) based on dry
107   weight, respectively (Table S1). The inoculum used in this study was sampled from a local
108   sewage treatment plant in Beijing, China. Before used, the inoculum was centrifuged at 5000
109   rpm for 10 min to concentrate, and then digested at 37 ± 1 °C for one week to exhaust the
110    residual biodegradable substances. The total solid (TS) and volatile solid (VS) of inoculum were
111   5.87 ± 0.17% and 2.77 ± 0.08%, respectively (Table S1).
112    2.2. Nanobubble preparation and characterization
113   Three gases, i.e. N2, H2, and CO2, were selected in this study to produce target nanobubble
114    solutions using a nanobubble generator purchased from Zhongnong Tianlu Company Ltd,
115    China. All gases (purity >99.9995%) were purchased from Beijing Haipu Gas CO., Ltd. During
116   the nanobubble generation process, gas and deionized water were pumped into the
117   nanobubble generator with inlet flow rates of 100 and 1000 L·h-1, respectively. The operation
118   time for the nanobubble generation was 15 mins, except for H2 (5 mins). The concentration
119   and average size of nanobubbles in the final solution were measured using the NanoSight
120   system (Nanoparticle tracking analysis, NTA NS500, Malvern Instrument Ltd. UK).
121    2.3. The effect of nanobubble treatment on AD of rice straw
122    2.3.1. Alterations in hydrolysis-acidification phases
123   The hydrolysis-acidification tests were conducted in AD reactors with a working volume of 200
124  mL for each. During the text, each reactor was loaded with 100 mL inoculum mixed with
125   deionised water (control group) or nanobubble (treatment groups), and rice straw with the
126    ratio of VSrice straw: VSinoculum=3:1 and adding 10 mM sodium 2-bromoethane sulfonate (BES)
127   (C2H4BrNaO3S) to inhibit methanogens [26]. As a result, the initial total VS in each reactor was
128   5.54 g·L-1. After well mixed, the sealed AD reactors were flushed by N2 for 5 mins to create
129   anaerobic conditions. Each control/treatment group was conducted with 3 parallel for 10 days,
130   and 3  bottles were removed  every two  days  for  sampling.  Notably,  although  the
131   methanogenesis was inhibited in this test, some gases (such as H2) could still be produced. The

132   volume of generated biogas was measured using a 50 mL air-tight glass syringe connected to
133   the headspace of each reactor. Then, 1 mL of biogas was collected for analysis the gas
134   components of H2, N2, CO2 and CH4 by a gas chromatograph (GC-8A, Shimadzu, Japan).
135   TS and VS were measured based on the standard methods [27]. pH was measured using a pH
136   meter (FE28, Mettler-Toledo, Switzerland). The original rice straw and solid residues were
137   subjected to morphological analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (S-4800, Hitachi,
138    Japan). Cellulose, hemicellulose, and acid detergent lignin contents were determined using a
139    fibre analyzer (2000, Ankon Techology Corp., USA) according to Van Soest [28]. Fourier
140   transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) were acquired using an FTIR spectrophotometer
141    (ALPHA-II) with a resolution of 4cm-1. Half amount of the samples was put into centrifuge at
142   10,000 rpm for 25 minutes, and the supernatant was filtered by 0.45 μm membrane filters
143   before the analysis. Soluble carbohydrates were quantified using Phenol-sulfuric acid method
144    [29]. SCOD was measured by Lianhua LH-DE500 reagent based on the fast digestion-
145   spectrophotometric method using a wavelength of 610nm. The gas chromatography (GC-2010
146    plus, Shimadu, Japan) was employed to determine the VFA concentrations. Samples were
147   taken from the reactor on finished to analyze the microbial community. The extraction,
148   sequencing, and analysis of the biological samples were meticulously carried out at Majorbio
149   Bio-pharm Technology. A comprehensive account of the specific steps and primers employed
150   can be found in the supplementary document. The operational taxonomic units (OTUs) and
151   the relative abundance of Bacteria were accurately derived from the 16S rRNA sequencing
152    data, ensuring precise taxonomic classification and quantification.

176    2.4. Statistical analysis
177   The statistical difference of the same parameters from different AD tests was analysed through
178    Kruskal-Wallis test using SPSS 22 (p < 0.05). Structural equation models were employed to

181   3. Results and discussion
182    3.1. Nanobubble characterizations
183   Various methods, including ethanol–water exchange, temperature change, electrochemical
184    reaction, and hydraulic cavitation, have been developed to produce nanobubbles [33]. The
185    hydraulic cavitation method is widely recognized as an effective approach, capable of rapidly
186   producing numerous nanobubbles (>107 bubbles·mL−1) within minutes [14,34], which was
187   used in this study. After operating the system for 15 mins, the system achieved concentrations
188    of N2 (Fig. 1a) and CO2 (Fig. 1b) nanobubbles at 1.43 × 108 and 5.46 × 107 bubbles·mL−1,
189    respectively. Although the generator is different, the obtained nanobubble concentrations
190    (107-108 bubbles·mL−1) were consistent with those reported in other studies using hydraulic
191    cavitation-based approaches [35]. As the operation time increased from 5 to 15 min, the
192   generated H2 nanobubble concentrations remained at the level of 107 bubbles·mL−1, which
193   may be due to the low viscosity, small molecular size, and high solubility of H2, which makes
194   H2 nanobubbles less stable. Therefore, a H2 nanobubble solution containing a concentration
195    of 4.04 × 107 bubbles·mL−1 (Fig. 1c) was used in this mechanistic exploration study. Additionally,
196   more than 99% of the nanobubbles in the three solutions exhibited a size below 400 nm.
197   Moreover, in addition to the formation of bubbles at the nanoscale, the process of generating
198   nanobubbles could lead to the (super) saturation of gas in the liquid solution as the
199   nanobubble slowly released the gas [36]. Therefore, the pH of the N2, CO2, and H2 nanobubble
200    solutions were 8.66 ± 0.23, 4.35 ± 0.08 and 5.50 ± 0.12, respectively.

203    3.2. Effect of nanobubble technology on the hydrolysis-acidification stage of AD of rice straw
204    3.2.1.  Solid phase – the structure of rice straw and lignocellulose contents
205   The changes of micro-structural arrangements occurred in rice straw after various gas
206   nanobubble pretreatments (Fig. 2). The surface of the pretreated rice straw exhibited a rugged,
207   rough texture with a high surface area, leading to changes in the stable agglomerated structure
208    of lignocellulose, while the surface of the control was even and smooth. The scanned surface
209    of untreated rice straw exhibited cracks to a certain extent and maintained a regular and
210   complete network structure. After treatment with H2 nanobubbles, the surface of rice straw
211    exhibited signs of loosened cell walls, characterized by channelling and peeling. In contrast,
212   the surfaces of rice straw treated with N2 and CO2 nanobubbles featured a higher porosity than
213   both H2 nanobubble-treated samples and the control. The destruction of the cell wall can be
214    attributed to the removal of lignin and the disruption of the lignocellulose complex structure
215    after nanobubble treatment. Thus, the surface areas accessible to enzymes increased, thereby
216   enhancing the convertibility of lignocellulosic biomass [37]. Nanobubbles with high mobility
217   can migrate from the bulk phase to the surface of cellulose particles, breaking through an
218    oligosaccharide layer that creates mass transfer resistance during the hydrolysis – acidification
219    of rice straw. These results indicated that all nanobubble treatments used in this study
220   disrupted the compact structure of rice straw, suggesting that  all of these treatments
221   enhanced the biodegradability of the rice straw to varying degrees.
222   During the hydrolysis and acidification of rice straw, the cellulose and hemicellulose contents
223    in the nanobubble treatment groups decreased to an average of 16.55% – 18.34% and 16.27%
224   –18.10%, respectively, compared with the control group (18.77%, and 17.19%). The percent
225    lignin content was higher in nanobubble treatment groups than in control group mainly due
226   to the lower degradation of lignin than other substances and the increased lignin resulting
227   from its concentration effect on the treated samples.
228   The FTIR spectra of deionized water, N2-, CO2- and H2-nanobubble treated rice straw were
229   analyzed (Figs. 2e and f). The results demonstrated that the spectra of rice straw treated with
230   deionized water and three types of nanobubbles exhibited similar profiles but with varying

                                           7

231    intensities of the absorption bands. Cellulose can exist in two forms, namely cellulose type I,
232   which  is the typical crystalline form, and cellulose type  II, which is the regenerated or
233   amorphous form. The absorption band at 1430 cm-1 indicated the presence of cellulose I,
234   which was highly resistant to biological digestibility. The absorption band at 896 cm−1 indicated
235   the presence of cellulose II, which was less resistant to enzymatic and microbial hydrolysis. The
236    lateral order index (LOI) was calculated using the absorbance ratio A1418/A893 [38,39]. The
237   LOI of control and N2-, CO2- and H2-nanobubble treatment groups were 0.76, 0.77, 0.85 and
238    0.74, respectively. This result indicates that N2- and CO2-nanobubbles could improve enzymatic
239   and microbial hydrolysis, resulting in increase of LOI. This result further validates the
240   conjecture of Wang and Sun [17], which suggested that nanobubbles could enhance the
241   degradation of amorphous cellulose. Notably, the absorption band at 1510 cm−1 was
242    attributable to the aromatic components in lignin. The nanobubble treatment group exhibited
243   lower absorbance than the control group. Previous research has revealed that nanobubble
244   generates reactive oxygen species (ROSs) when nanobubble collapses. The generation of •OH
245   through the use of nanobubble can aid in breaking C-C or C-O bonds present in lignin
246   molecules, resulting in the depolymerization of lignin. Additionally, this process can also target
247   the active sites on the benzene ring, leading to the opening of the ring [40].

252    3.2.2. Liquid phase – soluble organic matter
253   During the initial stage of AD, the solubilization hydrolysis reaction continuously hydrolyzes the
254    insoluble organic matter in rice straw into soluble organic matter. Subsequently, hydrolytic
255   enzymes degraded the complex organic substances, resulting in the production of soluble
256   carbohydrates, such as glucose. As indicated in Fig. 3a, SCOD concentration of CO2 nanobubble
257   treatment group increased faster compared to other treatments during the hydrolysis-
258    acidification stage, reaching a peak of 14740 ± 283 mg·L−1 on the 8th day. This indicated a 37.2%
                                           9

259    increase in SCOD of the treatment group compared with the control group (p < 0.05). The
260    increase in the SCOD concentration indicated the direct breakdown and efficient utilization of
261    organic materials by microorganisms [41]. The concentrations of soluble carbohydrates in the
262   nanobubble treatment groups were 6.27% (N2-nanobubble), 11.13% (CO2-nanobubble), 10.10%
263   (H2-nanobubble) higher than those in the control group on the 10th day (Fig.3b). These results
264   suggested  that the  addition  of CO2 and H2 nanobubbles  significantly enhanced the
265    solubilization of polysaccharides, while the effect of N2 nanobubbles on this enhancement was
266   minimal.

279    affected the VFAs ratio, such as the ratio of HBu to HAc (B/A ratio) and HPu to HAc (P/A ratio).

281    significant increase in B/A and P/A ratio were observed in the CO2 and H2 nanobubble
282   treatment group. This result suggests that treatment of N2 nanobubble did not modify the
283   metabolic pathway for hydrogen production, consistent with the findings from a previous
284   study [45]. Nevertheless, the CO2 and H2 nanobubble treatments could alter the metabolic
285   pathway for hydrogen production, shifting from HAc fermentation to HPu and HBu, which was

428    3.3.2. Kinetic analysis
429   The modified Gompertz model and the first-order kinetic model are commonly used to
430   describe the CH4 production kinetics in AD [55]. In this study, both models effectively simulated
431    (R2> 98%) the CH4 production dynamics from  all groups (Table 3). Consistent with the
432   cumulative CH4 production results (Fig. 8), the CO2 nanobubble treatment group exhibited the
433    highest maximum CH4 production rate (Rmax) at 14.95 mL·gVS−1·d−1 according to the Gompertz
434   model, which was 22.90% higher than that in the control group (11.74 mL·gVS−1·d−1).
435   Furthermore, the k value of the first-order model is another important parameter that directly
436    reflects the rate of hydrolysis, with a higher value meaning faster substrate hydrolysis [56]. The
437    fitting results revealed that k the control, CO2, N2, and H2 nanobubble treatment groups
438   featured k values of 0.042, 0.050, 0.055, and 0.045 d-1, respectively. These results indicate that
439   nanobubble technology can stimulate CH4 production and improve rice straw hydrolysis.
440   The lag time (λ) is a parameter that indicates the initial adaptability of microbes to the AD
441   system [55], and a lower λ value is more desirable as it improves the economic benefits of the
442    process. The nanobubble treatment resulted in a decrease in λ values, ranging from 0.88 to
443   1.06 days, compared with 1.09 days in the control group. This decrease indicated a quicker
444    start-up period for the rice straw AD process.

448    3.4. Implementation potential and research needs
449   The application of nanobubble technology in AD is an area of active research, but scientific
450   and technical challenges  still need to be addressed. Nanobubbles featured a negatively
451   charged zeta potential, which led to increased charge repulsion between particles, preventing
452    particle agglomeration [57]. Additionally, nanobubbles exhibited a longer spin–spin relaxation
453   time  (T2) than normal water molecules, which represents a higher water molecular
454    mobility[20]. This increased mobility can promote full contact between microorganisms and
455    organic matter, thereby facilitating nutrients transportation. Higher water mobility may
456   improve the fluidity of digested solutions and enhance mass transfer efficiency. In this study,
457   the effect of nanobubble on hydrogen production from rice straw hydrolysis was better than
458    that on methane production, indicating that nanobubbles altered the anaerobic digestion
459   pathway of rice straw, shifting it toward alcohol or other substances.
460    In terms of engineering applications, the use of reflux biogas slurry instead of water as the
461    carrier of nanobubbles will enhance the practicality of the process. This study shows that
462   nanobubble has a more obvious promotion effect on the hydrolytic acidification stage
463   compared with the methanogenesis stage. Therefore, nanobubbles should be used in the
464    hydrolytic acidification tank of two-phase anaerobic fermentation systems. In addition,
465   nanobubble  technology  can  significantly  promote  H2  production  during  anaerobic
466   fermentation. In the future, this technology can be used to improve the dark fermentation
467    process.  Certainly,  further  research can  investigate  the  feasibility and  efficiency  of
468   implementing this strategy in a full-scale, long-term anaerobic digestion system.

469   4. Conclusions
470    This study elucidated, the influence and mechanism of nanobubble treatment on the
471    hydrolysis-acidification and methane production processes during the AD of rice straw. The
472    result revealed that nanobubbles could enhance the hydrolysis and acidification stages of AD
473    of rice straw by disrupting the lignocellulosic material structure to produce higher levels of
474   SCOD, soluble carbohydrates, VFAs, and H2. Among the nanobubbles, the CO2-nanobubble
475    exhibited the highest significant effect on the acidification process. The microbial community

                                           18

476    analysis revealed that the CO2 nanobubble significantly increased the acidification-related
477    bacterial communities, such as Mobilitalea, unclassified_f_Lachnospiraceae, and Bacteroides.
478   Moreover, the introduction of CO2 nanobubbles improved the activity of hemicellulolytic
479   enzymes. Overall, the addition of nanobubbles facilitated the hydrolysis and acid production
480   process in the AD of rice straw and could serve as a green and effective method for rice straw
481   pretreatment to achieve more renewable energy during AD. The work of this article provides
482   support for the application of nanobubble technology in the field of renewable energy,
483    contributing to towards sustainable development goals.

727   Gas composition and other chemical compounds measurement
728    N2, CH4 and CO2 were measured daily with a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-8A, Japan). A
729   biogas sample of 0.5 mL was extracted from a biogas bag using a 1 mL gas-tight syringe and
730   subsequently introduced into the gas chromatograph. The gas chromatograph operated at
731   temperatures of 120 °C, 50 °C, and 120 °C for the inlet, column, and detector, respectively. A
732    stainless-steel column with dimensions of Φ10 m × 2 mm was employed, and the carrier gas
733    utilized was H2, maintained at a partial pressure of 0.38 MPa and a flow rate of 10–30 mL·min-
734     1. H2 was measured using a GC (Shimadzu GC-8A, Japan) with a 13X stainless steel molecular
735    sieve packed column (10 m × 2 mm). The temperatures of the thermal conductivity detector
736   and column oven were 120 °C and 60 °C, respectively. The volatile fatty acids (VFAs) were
737   analyzed using a GC (Shimadzu GC-2010 Plus, Japan) with a flame ionization detector and
738    capillary column of type Rtx-wax (30 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 μm). The column had an initial
739   temperature of 60 °C (5-min hold time), ramp10°C/min to 140 °C (2-min hold time), and ramp
740   20 °C/min to 230 °C (2-min hold time). The temperature of injector and detector were 230 °C
741   and 250 °C, respectively.
742   16rRNA gene sequencing and analysis
743     First, samples were thawed at room temperature. Subsequently, DNA was isolated using the
744    E.Z.N.A.® soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, U.S.). And the concentration and purity
745    of DNA were  determined  by 1%  agarose  gels  electrophoresis and NanoDrop2000
746   spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, United States) and kept at -80 °C prior to further use.
747   The  bacterial 16S rRNA gene were  amplified  with  bacterial primer  pair 338F  (50-
748   ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-30) and 806R (50-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-30). To distinguish
749   between different DNA samples, a distinctive barcode was allocated to the primer that
750   targeted each sample. For the amplification of bacterial DNA, the reaction mixtures were
751   composed of 10 ng of template DNA, 5 μmol of forward primer, 5 μmol of reverse primer, 0.4
752   μL of FastPfu Polymerase, 4 μL of 5 × FastPfu buffer, and 2.5 mmol/L of dNTP. Furthermore, in
753   order to ensure the stability and activity of the polymerase during the involvement of the
754   archaeal primer, a concentration of 0.2 μg/μL bovine serum albumin (BSA) was incorporated.
755   The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was initiated by subjecting the mixture to a denaturing
756   step at 95 °C for a duration of 3 minutes. Subsequently, a total of 27 cycles (using the bacterial
757   primer pair) were performed, consisting of 30 seconds at 95 °C, followed by 30 seconds at
758   55 °C, and finally, 45 seconds at 72 °C. To conclude the PCR process, an extension step at 72 °C
759    for 10 minutes was carried out. Then, the generated amplicons were extracted from 2%
760   agarose gels (AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction, Axygen Biosciences, USA), and quantified using
761   QuantiFluorTM-ST (Promega, USA). The upgraded amplicons were sequenced on the Illumina
762   platform (Majorbio Tech, China).
763   The raw FastQ files were subjected to quality filtration using QIIME software (version 1.17) to
764   ensure data integrity and reliability. Specifically, raw reads with a low quality score (<20) were
765   truncated from the beginning. Additionally, reads with a short length (<50 bp) were deemed
                                           27

766   inadequate and subsequently discarded. Furthermore, filtered sequences that exhibited an
767   overlap of more than 10 bp were assembled based on this overlap. Any reads containing
768   uncertain nucleotides or erroneous reads resulting from nucleotide mismatches in primer
769   adaptation were also eliminated from the analysis.
770   To obtain the operational taxonomic units (OTUs), the OTUs were initially clustered with the
771   software UPARSE. The chimeric sequences were identified and discarded using UCHIME. Then,
772   the trimmed reads were subsampled either for Bacteria or for Archaea, together with a
773    recalculation of the OTUs numbers. Subsequently, the taxonomy of each gene sequence was
774    identified by the software RDP Classifier against the SILVA v138 database with the 70%
775   confidence threshold. Identifications were ranked by tag abundance. Relative abundance was
776    calculated from the number of sequences that affiliated with a taxon divided by the total
777   number of sequences per sample.
